summary: Addresses how GMPLS and RSVP-TE apply to the overlay model, a user-network interface where clients request paths from a transport network without sharing routing information. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Some networks sit on top of a transport network and want paths through it without being told how it is built inside. This document explains how an edge node asks for such a path with RSVP-TE signalling, and what the transport network is allowed to do with the request.

questions: what is the gmpls overlay model
how does rsvp-te work between edge and core nodes
subtitle: How edge nodes ask a GMPLS core network for connections using RSVP-TE, without seeing inside the core.

tldr.problem: In a transport network built for GMPLS, the edge nodes of an overlay do not take part in the core's routing, so they have no view of the core's topology and no way to request a path across it.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines how RSVP-TE signalling works between an edge node and its adjacent core node: a single end-to-end RSVP session carries the user's parameters, the core computes or checks the route, and the edge node may include or omit the route and record objects as policy allows.
tldr.outcome: The overlay and the core can be independent of one another, which is what the automatically switched optical network architecture requires, and the same signalling can be used for private network connections.

sections.title: The Overlay Model
sections.content:
Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching defines both routing and signaling protocols for the creation of Label Switched Paths in various transport technologies. In a peer model, edge nodes support both a routing and a signaling protocol, and the protocol interactions between an edge node and a core node are the same as between two core nodes. In the overlay model, the core nodes act more as a closed system: the edge nodes do not participate in the routing protocol instance that runs among the core nodes, and in particular the edge nodes are unaware of the topology of the core nodes. There may, however, be a routing protocol interaction between a core node and an edge node for the exchange of reachability information to other edge nodes.

Figure 1 shows a reference network. The core network is the large box in the centre and contains five core nodes. The four boxes around the edge marked Overlay Network represent four islands of a single overlay network, and only the nodes with traffic-engineering links into the core network are shown; these are the edge nodes, and the terminology is in respect to the core network, not the overlay network. Each box marked Overlay Network could contain many other nodes; those nodes are not shown, do not participate directly in the signaling described in this document, and only the edge nodes can signal to set up links across the core to other edge nodes.

How a link between edge nodes is requested and triggered is out of the scope of the document, as is precisely how that link is used by the overlay network. One possibility is that the edge nodes inform the other nodes of the overlay network of the existence of the link. The document primarily addresses interactions between an edge node and its adjacent, at the data plane, core node; out-of-band and non-adjacent signaling capabilities may mean that signaling messages are delivered on a longer path. All signaling procedures are identical to the GMPLS extensions in RFC 3473, except as noted here.
sections.plainLanguage: The edge nodes are like tenants in a building: they can ask for a cable between two of their ports, but they cannot see the wiring in the walls and cannot route for themselves. The core nodes do the routing and say yes or no.

sections.title: The User-Network Interface
sections.content:
The GMPLS overlay model can be applied at the User-Network Interface reference point defined in the Automatically Switched Optical Network architecture. Consider the case where the core network in the reference model is a service provider network and the edge nodes are user devices. The interface between an edge node and a core node is the UNI reference point, and to support the ASON model, signaling across the UNI has to be defined.

The extensions provide mechanisms for UNI signaling that are compatible with GMPLS signaling in RFC 3471 and RFC 3473. They are also in line with the RSVP model: there is a single end-to-end RSVP session for the user connection, the first and last hops constitute the UNI, and the RSVP session carries the user parameters end to end. This obviates the need to map user parameters to the format expected by the network-to-network interface used inside the service provider network, which in turn means the UNI and the NNI can be independent of one another, a requirement of the ASON architecture. In the case where the UNI and NNI are both GMPLS and RSVP-based, the methodology allows a single RSVP session to instantiate both UNI and NNI signaling, if desired and if allowed by service provider policy.

Realization of a single or multiple instance of the UNI is implementation dependent at both the core node and the edge node, so long as it meets the functional requirements for robustness, security and privacy set out in the document's VPN section.
sections.plainLanguage: One signalling session runs from one edge node to the other, and it carries the user's own parameters the whole way. That means the network's internal interface does not have to be reshaped to fit the user's request.

sections.title: How the Edge Nodes Are Addressed
sections.content:
Addresses for edge nodes in the overlay model are drawn from the same address space the edge nodes use to address their adjacent core nodes. This may be the same space the core nodes use among themselves, or it may be a VPN space that the core nodes support as an overlay.

More specifically, an edge node and its attached core node must share the same address space used by GMPLS to signal between edge nodes across the core network. A set of edge-node and core-node tuples share the same address space if the edge nodes in the set could establish label switched paths through the core nodes among themselves without address mapping or translation, and the edge nodes in the set may be a subset of all the edge nodes. The address space the core nodes use among themselves may, but need not, be shared with the address space used by any of those tuples. This does not imply a mandatory one-to-one mapping between a set of LSPs and a given addressing space.

When multiple overlay networks are supported by a single core network, one or more address spaces may be used according to privacy requirements. This may be achieved without varying the core node addresses, since it is the edge-node and core-node tuple that constitutes address space membership.

An edge node is identified by either a single IP address representing its Node-ID, or by one or more numbered traffic-engineering links that connect it to the core nodes. Core nodes are assumed to be ignorant of any other addresses associated with an edge node, that is, addresses not used in signaling connections through the GMPLS core. An edge node needs to know only its own address, an address of the adjacent core node, and the address of any other edge node it wishes to connect to, as well as the addresses used in the overlay network island of which it is part. A core node needs to know and track only the addresses on interfaces between it and its attached edge nodes, the Node IDs of those edge nodes, and the interface addresses and Node IDs of other edge nodes that an attached edge node is permitted to connect to.

When forming a SENDER_TEMPLATE, the ingress edge node includes either its Node-ID or the address of one of its numbered traffic-engineering links, in which case the connection will only be made over that interface. When forming a SESSION_OBJECT, the ingress edge node includes either the Node-ID of the egress edge device or the address of one of the egress's numbered traffic-engineering links, and again the connection will only be made over that interface. The Extended_Tunnel_ID of the session object is set to either zero or to an address of the ingress edge device.
sections.plainLanguage: An edge node is named by one address, or by the particular link it wants the connection to leave from. The core only needs to know the addresses of the edge nodes directly attached to it, and it never needs to know the rest of an edge node's addresses.

sections.title: Route and Record Objects
sections.content:
An edge node MAY include an explicit route object in its Path message, and a core node MAY reject a Path message that contains one. Such behaviour is controlled by configuration. If a core node rejects a Path message because of the presence of an ERO, it SHOULD return a PathErr message with an error code of Unknown object class toward the sender, which causes the path setup to fail. A core node MAY accept EROs that only include the ingress edge node, the ingress core node, the egress core node and the egress edge node; this supports explicit label control on the edge node interface. If it rejects a Path message because of an ERO that is not of the permitted format, it SHOULD return a PathErr message with an error code of Bad Explicit Route Object.

When a core node receives a Path message from an edge node that contains no ERO, it MUST calculate a route to the destination and include that route in an ERO before forwarding the Path message. The exception is when the egress edge node is also adjacent to this core node. If no route can be found, the core node SHOULD return a PathErr message with an error code and value of 24,5, No route available toward destination.

When a core node receives a Path message that contains an ERO, it SHOULD verify the route against its topology database before forwarding the Path message. If the route is not viable, according to topology, currently available resources or local policy, a PathErr message with an error code and value of 24,5 should be returned.

For explicit label control and full identification of the egress link, an ingress edge node may include this information in the ERO it passes to its neighbouring core node. In the case that no other ERO is supplied, the explicit control information is provided as the only hop of the ERO and is encoded by setting the first subobject of the ERO to the node-ID of the egress core node with the L-bit set; following this subobject are all other subobjects necessary to identify the link and labels as they would normally appear. The same rules apply to the explicit control subobjects as the last hop in the ERO when a fuller ERO is supplied, but in this case the L-bit MAY be clear.

An edge node MAY include a recorded route object. A core node MAY remove the RRO from the Path message before forwarding it, and MAY remove it from a Resv message before forwarding it to the edge node. A core node MAY also edit the RRO in a Resv message so that it includes only the subobjects from the egress core node through the egress edge node, which allows the ingress node to be aware of the selected link and labels at the far end of the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: An edge node may suggest the route it wants the core to take, or leave the choice to the core. If it suggests one, the core checks it against its own map and current capacity and can refuse. The core can also trim the record of the route it actually took before handing it back.

sections.title: Notifications Between Edge and Core
sections.content:
An edge node MAY include a NOTIFY_REQUEST object in both the Path and Resv messages it generates, and core nodes may send Notify messages to edge nodes that have included such an object. A core node MAY remove a NOTIFY_REQUEST object from a Path or Resv message received from an edge node before forwarding it. If no NOTIFY_REQUEST object is present in the Path or Resv received from an edge node, the core node adjacent to the edge node may include one and set its value to its own address.

In either of these cases, the core node SHOULD NOT send Notify messages to the edge node. When a core node receives a NOTIFY_REQUEST object from an edge node, it MAY update the Notify Node Address with its own address before forwarding it, in which case Notify messages received later MAY be selectively forwarded to the edge node based on local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: An edge node can ask to be told about problems on its connection. The core node usually absorbs that request rather than passing it on, and sends the notifications itself, so that the core's internal nodes are not asked to report on parts of the network the edge node knows nothing about.

sections.title: Deleting a Connection
sections.content:
RSVP-TE deletes connections using either a single pass PathTear message, or a ResvTear and PathTear message combination. On receipt of the PathTear message a node deletes the connection state and forwards the message. In optical networks, however, deleting a connection at a node, for example removing the cross-connect, may cause the connection to be perceived as failed in downstream nodes, with loss of frame or loss of light, which may in turn lead to management alarms and perhaps the triggering of restoration or protection for the connection.

To address this, the graceful connection deletion procedure SHOULD be followed. Under it, an ADMIN_STATUS object MUST be sent in a Path or Resv message along the connection's path to inform all nodes en route that the connection is about to be deleted, before the actual deletion. If an ingress core node receives a PathTear without having first seen an ADMIN_STATUS object, it MAY pause the PathTear and first send a Path message with an ADMIN_STATUS object to inform all downstream label switching routers that the connection is about to be deleted. When the Resv is received echoing the ADMIN_STATUS, or a timer is used, the ingress core node MUST forward the PathTear.

RFC 3473 introduces a Path_State_Removed flag in a PathErr message, indicating that the sender has removed all state associated with the LSP and does not need to see a PathTear. A core node next to an edge node MAY map between teardown using ResvTear and PathTear and PathErr with Path_State_Removed. A core node next to an edge node that receives a ResvTear from its downstream neighbour MAY respond with a PathTear and send a PathErr with Path_State_Removed further upstream. However, a core node next to an edge node that receives a PathErr with Path_State_Removed from its downstream neighbour MUST NOT retain Path state and send a ResvTear further upstream, because that would imply that Path state further downstream had also been retained.
sections.plainLanguage: Tearing a connection down in an optical network can look like a failure to the next node along, which sets off alarms and possibly triggers a backup path. So the network is warned first, and only then is the connection removed.

sections.title: Private Network Connections
sections.content:
The extensions are designed to be compatible with the support of VPNs. Since the core network may be some technology other than GMPLS, no mandatory means of mapping core connections to access connections is specified. However, when GMPLS is used for the core network, it is RECOMMENDED that a procedure based on the LSP hierarchy be followed.

The VPN connection is modelled as being three hops: one for each access link and one hop across the core network. The VPN connection is established using a two-step procedure. When a Path message is received at a core node on an interface that is part of a VPN, the Path message is held until a core connection is established. The connection across the core is set up as a separate signaling exchange between the core nodes, using the address space of the core nodes, and while that exchange is in progress the original Path message is held at the ingress core node. Once the exchange for the core connection is complete, this connection is used in the VPN connection as if it were a single link, signalled by including an IF_ID RSVP_HOP object. The original Path message is then forwarded within the VPN addressing realm to the core node attached to the destination edge node. Many ways of accomplishing this are available, including IP and GRE tunnels and BGP/MPLS VPNs; specifying a particular means is beyond the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: A private network connection is treated as three hops: into the core, across it, and out again. The core builds its own connection first, then stitches the user's request onto it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The trust model between the core and edge nodes is different from the one described in RFC 3473, because the core is permitted to hide its topology from the edge nodes, and the core is permitted to restrict the actions of edge nodes by filtering out specific RSVP objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The edge node trusts the core to keep its topology secret and to enforce policy by dropping parts of the request. That is a different arrangement from the ordinary GMPLS signalling trust model, and the document says so without spelling out further consequences.
